section_summary: This section comprises diplomatic despatches, telegrams, memoranda, letters, and cross-reference sheets from April to November 1933 detailing Japan's internal political strife, Cabinet tensions, and foreign policy reassessment following its departure from the League of Nations. It highlights the endurance of the non-partisan Saito Cabinet amid bitter struggles between civilian ministers and the military over the state budget, as well as Japanese anxieties concerning potential United States-Soviet rapprochement. Additionally, the section documents right-wing extremist unrest, including the abortive Shinheitai conspiracy and the sensational public trials of the Blood Brotherhood and May 15, 1932 conspirators, which severely undermined parliamentary party government and inflamed anti-treaty chauvinism.

subfiles.about: Ambassador Grew reports on predictions by Japanese liberal thinkers that chauvinism will give way to international conciliation, but notes that military dominance makes such optimism premature.
subfiles.summary: Telegram No. 80: moderates, reflecting Saionji, expect international cooperation to follow the chauvinist wave. Grew advises these hopes merit attention, but not reliance, under military control.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 80 (Sections 2 and 3) from Tokyo regarding Japanese Moderates and Foreign Policy

subfiles.about: Vice President Frank C. Page of ITT transmits monthly situation reports on Tokyo and Scandinavia to Under-Secretary of State Phillips.
subfiles.summary: Page forwards ITT managers' reports: Tokyo on the 64th Diet and 2.23 billion yen budget; Scandinavia on Norway's government change and Danish currency and tariff measures.
subfiles.title: Letter from Frank C. Page Transmitting ITT Managers' Reports on Tokyo and the Scandinavian District

subfiles.about: A State Department charge slip recording the temporary transfer of an enclosure from decimal file 894.00/479 to officer Harley.
subfiles.summary: Charge slip showing an enclosure to file 894.00/479 charged out to SPA-Harley on February 17, 1945.
subfiles.title: Charge Slip for Enclosure to File 894.00/479

subfiles.about: Ambassador Grew reports on the arrest of 49 members of the reactionary 'Godly Soldiers' (Shinheitai) of the Dai-Nippon Seisanto plotting terroristic attacks and assassinations.
subfiles.summary: Despatch No. 474 details the arrest of 49 members of the 'Dai Nippon Shin-heitai' (Godly Soldiers), affiliated with the Dai-Nippon Seisanto and Black Dragon Society, at the Meiji Shrine on July 10-11, 1933. The group planned a terror campaign targeting Premier Saito, party leaders, and War Minister General Araki, who had frustrated military extremists by restraining violence and supporting the Cabinet. Grew notes that the plot was poorly equipped with only three swords and gasoline, leading observers to view it as either a bid for notoriety or a warning to courts trying the May 15, 1932 conspirators. A formal summary sheet is attached on page 240.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 474 from Tokyo: Recrudescence of Reactionary Activities

subfiles.about: C. Inman Barnard sends a press clipping from Excelsior featuring Pierre Mille's analysis of Andrée Viollis's book on Japan's political crisis and war danger.
subfiles.summary: Barnard sends the White House an Excelsior article by Pierre Mille on Viollis's book: Japan hovers between military fascism and foreign war. Referred to State on August 22, 1933.
subfiles.title: Letter from C. Inman Barnard Enclosing Newspaper Clipping from Excelsior on Japan's Internal Crisis

subfiles.about: C. Inman Barnard forwards a clipping from Le Temps containing an analysis by André Duboscq on Japanese-American naval rivalry and aviation, alongside reports on Nazi Germany.
subfiles.summary: C. Inman Barnard transmits an issue of Le Temps dated July 27, 1933 to the White House. The lead article by André Duboscq examines General Italo Balbo's mass flight to North America, arguing that modern aviation erases natural geographical insulation and warning that close economic ties between the United States and Japan will not avert a Pacific conflict. The accompanying newspaper text also includes reports from Germany on compulsory eugenic sterilization, Nordic-centric history education directives by Interior Minister Frick, and Catholic ceremonies at Trier.
subfiles.title: Letter from C. Inman Barnard Enclosing Newspaper Clipping from Le Temps on Japanese-American Relations and Italo Balbo's Flight

subfiles.about: A State Department Division of Far Eastern Affairs memorandum analyzing Tokyo Despatch No. 497 and concurring on the likely longevity of the Saito Cabinet.
subfiles.summary: Dooman agrees the Embassy is right that the Saito Cabinet will endure without major change, though Japanese political forecasting is difficult.
subfiles.title: Memorandum by Division of Far Eastern Affairs regarding Tokyo Despatch No. 497 on the Saito Cabinet

subfiles.about: Counselor Neville reports on the resilience of the Saito coalition government, widespread public contempt for political parties, and plans to strengthen the Ministry.
subfiles.summary: Despatch No. 497 examines the stability of the Saito coalition Cabinet formed in the wake of the May 15, 1932 assassination of Premier Inukai. Although the majority Seiyukai party desires a return to single-party government, public hostility toward partisan corruption—heightened by the eloquent anti-parliamentary testimony of defendants in the ongoing May 15 trials—prevents any change. To fortify the government prior to Diet debates on heavy military appropriations, proposals have emerged to invite party leaders Dr. Kisaburo Suzuki and Baron Reijiro Wakatsuki into the Cabinet as ministers without portfolio, while Finance Minister Takahashi warns that public disgust with politicians could trigger a military dictatorship. A summary sheet is included on page 259.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 497 from Tokyo: The Saito Government and the Political Parties

subfiles.about: A cross-reference sheet noting that Tokyo Despatch No. 491 concerning Japanese press speculation on foreign policy was filed under 794.00/57.
subfiles.summary: Cross-references Despatch No. 491 (794.00/57), August 9, 1933: Japanese newspaper stories proposing new foreign policies.
subfiles.title: Document File Note Cross-Referencing Despatch No. 491 on Japanese Foreign Policy

subfiles.about: Ambassador Grew analyzes Japanese press agitation for an independent Asiatic diplomacy, an offensive-defensive alliance with China, and regional hegemony.
subfiles.summary: Despatch No. 491 surveys Japanese press reactions to international isolation following Japan's withdrawal from the League of Nations and British imperial trade restrictions. Influenced by returning diplomats like Yosuke Matsuoka, newspapers criticized the Foreign Office's 'subservient diplomacy' and publicized proposals for a Sino-Japanese bloc and an offensive-defensive alliance modeled on the Manchukuo protocol, echoing the Twenty-One Demands. Press outlets such as Yomiuri and Kokumin promoted Pan-Asian resistance against Western white exploitation, while attacking Count Uchida's passivity. Grew concludes that while much of this commentary is speculative, it reflects deep national anxiety and underscores that Japan's primary objective remains securing Manchuria to dominate Asia.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 491 from Tokyo: Foreign Policy of Japan

subfiles.about: A cross-reference sheet and attached extract from Tokyo Periodic Report No. 88 detailing the Shinheitai assassination conspiracy against government leaders.
subfiles.summary: Extract from Despatch No. 490: 108 Dai-Nippon Seisanto members arrested July 1933 plotting an Imperial Way coup targeting statesmen, financiers and War Minister Araki.
subfiles.title: Document File Note and Extract from Despatch No. 490 on the Shinheitai Assassination Plot

subfiles.about: A State Department desk memorandum summarizing Peiping Despatch No. 2265 and Minister Johnson's doubts regarding an imminent Japanese invasion of North China.
subfiles.summary: Dooman summarizes Peiping Despatch No. 2265: rumors from Kailan officials that the Japanese Army would occupy Peiping and Tientsin; Minister Johnson doubts any imminent invasion.
subfiles.title: Memorandum by Division of Far Eastern Affairs regarding Peiping Despatch No. 2265 on Japanese Intentions in North China

subfiles.about: Minister Johnson transmits a memorandum of conversation with Military Attaché Colonel Drysdale regarding rumors of an impending Japanese advance on Peiping and Tientsin.
subfiles.summary: Kailan Mining officials say Kwantung Army officers plan to advance south of the Great Wall. Johnson doubts it, since Japan could have taken Peiping three months earlier.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 2265 from Peiping: Future Plans of Japan

subfiles.about: A cross-reference sheet indicating that Tokyo Despatch No. 515 on General Araki's political ambitions was filed under 033.9411 Shiratori, Toshio/5.
subfiles.summary: Cross-references Despatch No. 515 (033.9411 Shiratori, Toshio/5), September 12, 1933: rumors that Araki's followers intend to force a cabinet change and overturn party government.
subfiles.title: Document File Note Cross-Referencing Despatch No. 515 on General Araki and Toshio Shiratori

subfiles.about: Ambassador Grew reports on Toshio Shiratori's travel through America and persistent rumors of military pressure by General Araki for a totalitarian reorganization of Japan.
subfiles.summary: Despatch No. 515 discusses the transit through the United States of Toshio Shiratori, newly appointed Minister to Sweden and close ally of Japanese military extremists. Shiratori hinted at impending radical domestic changes, coinciding with General Araki's proposals to Finance Minister Takahashi to reorganize Japan along Nazi lines by dissolving political parties, establishing a single national party, rejecting Western ideologies, and expanding military control. Grew also mentions unverified rumors that Emperor Hirohito might abdicate in favor of Prince Chichibu if the expectant Empress fails to deliver a male heir, and reiterates warnings by Takahashi that failure of the political parties could precipitate a feudal military dictatorship.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 515 from Tokyo: Rumors in connection with Mr. Toshio Shiratori's visit to America

subfiles.about: Ambassador Grew reports severe Cabinet discord as Foreign Minister Hirota joins Finance Minister Takahashi in resisting the military's exorbitant budget demands.
subfiles.summary: Reports Cabinet dispute over military appropriations: Hirota allies with Finance Minister Takahashi against excess spending. Militarists might stage a coup and force Saito to resign.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 156 from Tokyo: Cabinet Disagreement over Military Appropriations

subfiles.about: A cross-reference sheet indicating that an FE memorandum by Stanley K. Hornbeck on current Japanese politics and Count Soyeshima was filed under 033.9411/287.
subfiles.summary: Cross-references Hornbeck's September 16, 1933 memorandum (033.9411/287) on Japanese politics and Count Soyeshima's attitude.
subfiles.title: Document File Note Cross-Referencing Memorandum on Japanese Politics and Count Soyeshima

subfiles.about: Ambassador Grew reports an emerging Cabinet compromise granting the military funds for equipment renewal while adopting Hirota's premise that Japan faces no imminent attack.
subfiles.summary: Reports a Cabinet compromise: the military gets most funds justified by modernization, not threat, a Hirota victory. The military agrees to moderate its rhetoric, improving Saito's prospects.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 164 from Tokyo: Cabinet Compromise on Military Budget

subfiles.about: A State Department summary paraphrase of Telegram No. 164 outlining the Cabinet budget settlement between Foreign Minister Hirota and the military.
subfiles.summary: Departmental paraphrase of Telegram No. 164: military budget agreed on technical grounds with Hirota's view that Japan faces no attack, easing militarism and strengthening Saito.
subfiles.title: Summary Paraphrase of Telegram No. 164 from Tokyo on Cabinet Budget Agreement

subfiles.about: A cross-reference sheet indicating that Telegram No. 166 concerning the effect of US-Soviet talks on the Japanese military budget was filed under 711.61/293.
subfiles.summary: Cross-references Telegram No. 166 (711.61/293), October 24, 1933: effects of US-Soviet negotiations on the Japanese military budget.
subfiles.title: Document File Note Cross-Referencing Telegram No. 166 on US-Soviet Negotiations and the Japanese Budget

subfiles.about: Ambassador Grew reports Foreign Office anxieties that US-Soviet diplomatic rapprochement might be misconstrued and provoke a militarist backlash in Japan.
subfiles.summary: Kurusu tells Neville the Foreign Office fears US-Soviet talks suggest American backing against Japan, feeding military claims of encirclement and undermining Hirota's calming of chauvinism.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 166 from Tokyo: Japanese Reactions to US-Soviet Negotiations

subfiles.about: A State Department routing memorandum accompanying Tokyo Despatch No. 565 on reactionary assassinations and trials.
subfiles.summary: Cover memorandum by Dooman for Despatch No. 565, a full account of the 1932 political assassinations and trials.
subfiles.title: Memorandum by Division of Far Eastern Affairs regarding Tokyo Despatch No. 565 on Reactionary Trials

subfiles.about: Ambassador Grew transmits an extensive report on the trials of the Blood Brotherhood and May 15, 1932 conspirators, analyzing the ideological roots of reactionary terrorism.
subfiles.summary: Despatch No. 565 transmits the introductory sections of an Embassy study on the public trials of reactionary conspirators involved in the 1932 assassinations. Grew analyzes how the government's decision to stage-manage high-profile public trials backfired by generating broad popular sympathy for the defendants' self-sacrificing patriotism, while dealing a devastating blow to parliamentary parties (Seiyukai and Minseito) and popularizing opposition to the London Naval Treaty. The enclosed report explores the cultural and military origins of extremist violence, cites War Minister Araki's philosophy on military moral superiority, and chronicles the assassinations of former Finance Minister Junnosuke Inouye and Baron Takuma Dan by the Blood Brotherhood, leading up to the May 15, 1932 assault that claimed Premier Inukai's life.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 565 from Tokyo: Transmitting Report on the Reactionary Trials
